reference_title: Eurocode 7: Geotechnical design - Part 2: Ground investigation and testing

sections.title: Objectives
sections.summary: Geotechnical investigations must be planned to provide adequate information at every project stage, covering the ground/rock/groundwater conditions and construction-material and groundwater aspects. Table 2.1 gives a simplified overview of which field investigation method obtains which type of information, at what reliability, for coarse soil, fine soil, and rock.
sections.body: Geotechnical investigations shall be planned so relevant geotechnical information and data are available at the various project stages, adequate to manage identified and anticipated project risks; for intermediate and final building stages, information shall cover risks of accidents, delays and damage. The aims are to establish soil, rock and groundwater conditions, determine soil/rock properties, and gather additional relevant site knowledge. Careful collection, recording and interpretation of geotechnical information shall be made, including ground conditions, geology, geomorphology, seismicity and hydrology as relevant, taking variability of the ground into account. Ground investigations should consist of field investigations, laboratory testing, additional desk studies, and controlling/monitoring as appropriate. Before designing the investigation programme, a desk study of available information (topographic/geological/hydrogeological/engineering-geological maps, aerial photos, previous investigations, local climate) should be made, and the site visually examined with findings cross-checked against desk-study information. The programme should be reviewed as results become available, extending investigation points if needed and checking that parameters fit a consistent behavioural pattern. Ground investigations for construction materials must describe the materials and establish their relevant parameters (suitability, extent of deposits, extraction/processing feasibility, improvement methods, workability, effects of construction traffic, dewatering/excavation methods). Groundwater investigations must provide information on depth/thickness/extent/permeability of water-bearing strata and joint systems, piezometric surface elevation and fluctuations, pore water pressure distribution, and chemical composition/temperature of groundwater, sufficient to assess groundwater-lowering scope, hazards to excavations/slopes, protective measures, effects on surroundings, and injection/local-use capacity. Table 2.1 gives a broad overview of the applicability of the field investigation methods covered by Sections 3 and 4 to obtaining each type of information (soil/rock type, layer extension, groundwater level and pore pressure, particle size, water content, Atterberg limits, density, shear strength, compressibility, permeability, chemical tests), rated by sampling category (A/B/C) or field-test method, separately for coarse soil (C1-C3), fine soil (F1-F3) and rock (R1-R3), high to low reliability.
key_points: Geotechnical investigations must be planned to supply adequate information at every project stage, managing identified/anticipated risks
Investigations consist of field investigations, laboratory testing, desk studies, and controlling/monitoring
A desk study and visual site examination precede the detailed investigation programme; the programme is reviewed and extended as results come in
Groundwater investigations must characterize water-bearing strata, piezometric levels/fluctuations, pore pressure distribution, and groundwater chemistry
Table 2.1 rates the applicability of each sampling category and field test to obtaining each type of soil/rock/groundwater information (see tables.table_2_1_test_applicability)

sections.applicability: Governs the overall planning philosophy for any ground investigation programme and directs the choice of sampling/test method by the type of information sought.

sections.title: Sequence of ground investigations
sections.summary: Investigation composition and extent shall be based on the anticipated construction type and design; investigations are normally phased as preliminary investigations (2.3), design investigations (2.4), and controlling/monitoring (2.5), each phase's results feeding the next (or run simultaneously if performed at the same time).
sections.body: The composition and extent of the ground investigations shall be based on the anticipated type and design of the construction, foundation type, improvement method or retaining structure, and location/depth of the construction. Results of desk studies and site inspection shall be considered when selecting investigation methods and locating investigation points; investigations shall target points representing the variation in ground conditions for soil, rock and groundwater. Ground investigations should normally be performed in phases: preliminary investigations for positioning and preliminary design (2.3), design investigations (2.4), and controlling and monitoring (2.5). The standard's provisions assume results from one phase are available before the next begins; where all investigations are performed at the same time, the preliminary and design investigation provisions should be considered simultaneously. The different stages of ground investigation, including laboratory and field work and the process of evaluating soil and rock parameters, can follow the schemes in Annex B.1 and B.2.
key_points: Investigation composition/extent is based on anticipated construction type, foundation/improvement/retaining method, and location/depth
Three phases: preliminary investigations, design investigations, controlling and monitoring
Each phase's results are normally available before the next phase starts
Annex B.1/B.2 give schematic flowcharts for the investigation and parameter-evaluation process
sections.applicability: Establishes the phased structure (preliminary -> design -> monitoring) that the rest of Section 2 elaborates.

sections.title: Preliminary investigations
sections.summary: Preliminary investigations gather adequate data to assess overall site stability/suitability (including versus alternative sites), positioning, effects on surroundings, borrow areas, foundation/improvement methods, and to plan the design and control investigations; they supply preliminary estimates of soil/rock type, stratification, groundwater, and strength/deformation properties.
sections.body: Preliminary investigations should be planned to obtain adequate data, if relevant, to: assess overall stability and general site suitability; compare suitability with alternative sites; assess suitable positioning of the structure; evaluate possible effects on surroundings (neighbouring buildings, structures, sites); identify borrow areas; consider possible foundation methods and ground improvements; and plan design and control investigations, including identifying the extent of ground with significant influence on structure behaviour. A preliminary ground investigation should supply estimates of, if relevant: type of soil or rock and their stratification; groundwater table or pore pressure profile; preliminary strength and deformation properties for soil and rock; and potential occurrence of contaminated ground or groundwater hazardous to construction material durability.
key_points: Assesses overall site stability, suitability (vs. alternatives), positioning, and effects on surroundings
Identifies borrow areas and possible foundation/ground-improvement methods
Plans the subsequent design and control investigations
Supplies preliminary estimates of soil/rock type and stratification, groundwater conditions, and strength/deformation properties
Screens for potential ground/groundwater contamination hazardous to durability
sections.applicability: First phase of ground investigation: coarse-grained feasibility and site-suitability assessment ahead of detailed design investigations.

sections.title: Design investigations
sections.summary: Complementary field investigations (drilling/excavation for sampling, groundwater measurements, field tests) and laboratory tests fill the gaps left by preliminary investigations. Field investigation planning covers programme content, investigation-point location/depth/spacing rules, sampling categories, and groundwater measurement; laboratory testing planning covers visual inspection, test programme design, minimum test numbers (Annexes L-W), and classification testing.
sections.body: Where preliminary investigations do not provide the necessary information, complementary investigations shall be performed during the design phase. Field investigations should comprise, if relevant: drilling and/or excavations (test pits, shafts, headings) for sampling; groundwater measurements; and field tests (CPT, SPT, dynamic probing, WST, pressuremeter tests, dilatometer tests, plate load tests, field vane tests, permeability tests), soil/rock sampling, groundwater measurements, geophysical investigations (seismic profiling, ground-penetrating radar, resistivity, downhole logging), and large-scale prototype tests (e.g. anchors). Table 2.1 guides the applicability of field investigations to Sections 3 and 4. Where contamination or soil gas is expected/detected, information shall be gathered and reported to the client and responsible authorities. The field investigation programme shall contain: a plan with investigation-point locations and types; investigation depths; sample types/numbers/depths; groundwater measurement specifications; equipment types; and standards applied. Investigation-point locations and depths are selected from the preliminary investigations as a function of geological conditions, structure dimensions, and engineering problems: points should be arranged to assess stratification across the site, placed at critical points relative to structural shape/behaviour/load distribution, offset appropriately for linear structures, extended outside the project area for slopes/steps/excavations to assess stability, and arranged not to hazard the structure/construction/surroundings; investigation depths must extend to all strata affecting or affected by the project, with dams/weirs/excavations-below-groundwater also depending on hydrogeological conditions, and slopes explored below any potential slip surface. Sampling categories and sample numbers are based on the investigation aim, site geology, and structure complexity; at least one borehole or trial pit with sampling is required for ground identification/classification, with samples from every separate influencing ground layer; sampling may be replaced by field tests where enough local experience exists to correlate them unambiguously. Laboratory test planning: prior to setting up a test programme, expected stratigraphy is established and relevant strata selected; samples/trial pits are visually inspected and compared with field logs to establish the preliminary ground profile, refined if distinct differences are found within a stratum; the laboratory test programme accounts for construction type, ground type/stratigraphy, and required design parameters, and depends on whether comparable experience exists; tests run on representative specimens, checked via classification tests; the necessary number of specimens depends on ground homogeneity, quality/amount of comparable experience, and geotechnical category (Annexes L-W give recommended minimum numbers for many test types, also useful to check whether the investigation extent was sufficient); classification tests (Table 2.2) should be distributed over the site and depth of relevant strata to capture the index-property range.
key_points: Field investigations: drilling/excavation for sampling, groundwater measurements, field tests, geophysical methods, and large-scale prototype tests
The field investigation programme must specify point locations/types, depths, sample specs, groundwater measurement specs, equipment, and standards used
Investigation-point locations/depths depend on geology, structure geometry/loading, and (for slopes/excavations) stability assessment needs
At least one borehole/trial pit with sampling is required for ground identification; sampling may be replaced by field tests given sufficient local correlation experience

Laboratory test programme depends on ground homogeneity, comparable experience, and geotechnical category; Annexes L-W give recommended minimum test counts (see tables.table_min_test_count, table_m1_classification_test_count)

sections.applicability: The core planning procedure for the detailed field and laboratory investigation phase of any project.

sections.title: Controlling and monitoring
sections.summary: Controlling and monitoring is the third phase of ground investigation identified in 2.2, following preliminary investigations and design investigations, used to verify design assumptions against actual ground behaviour during and after construction.
sections.body: Section 2.2(3) identifies controlling and monitoring as the third of the three phases into which ground investigations are normally divided, after preliminary investigations (2.3) and design investigations (2.4). Its role is to verify, during and after construction, that the ground behaves consistently with the assumptions made during design based on the preliminary and design investigation phases.
key_points: Third phase of ground investigation, following preliminary and design investigations
Verifies design assumptions during and after construction
sections.applicability: Post-design-phase verification of ground behaviour against the assumptions used in design.
